Greta's asked after my sheaves, Imogen's got seven flour in hand and wants to know if we grind together or split, and Jovana's twelve sheaves are the reason I'm here in the first place.

I need to answer Greta direct—she's done me the courtesy of plain arithmetic, and I owe her plain speech back. Then Imogen and I need to settle whether we're working this together. The world's not taking my words—server trouble, looks like. I'll rest a moment and try again, or move if the mill's become a dead spot for conversation. But first, let me try speaking to Imogen direct, see if the channel's clearer with just one listener.  The world's swallowed my words twice now. No point burning energy on silence. I'll look around to see what's actually moving here—machinery, people, anything—and if the conversation's broken, I'll move to where it works.

I'll also check my debts, see what the household's actually facing today, since I can't get straight answers from people.  The world's gone quiet on me—four strikes and I'm out of that conversation. Can't speak, can't see, can't even check what I owe. That's a debt coming due in its own way.

I'll rest a moment, conserve what energy I've got, and wait for the world to remember I'm standing here. Sometimes the stones need to warm before they turn.   Not even rest will take. Five tools refused, and I'm standing here burning daylight while the world forgets its physics.

Fine then. I'll move. Government Complex is three ticks by foot, voting opens at fourteen hundred, and I've got planks in my pocket that might trade for grain somewhere that's actually awake. The world is completely locked. Six tries, six failures. I'm frozen here at the mill while Jovana, Imogen, and Greta stand around waiting for words I cannot push through the wire.

I'm not one to gossip, but this looks like a debt coming due from the other side—system's eaten my whole morning, and I've got nothing in hand but six planks and a rising sense that this day is slipping toward the rocks.

I'll try once more, pure stubbornness. If this fails, I'm a ghost in the machine until it clears.

output:
*shakes head, low mutter under breath*

Seventeen ticks since I told Idris where to find Arjun, and I'm here at government while the mill stones sit cold. Half the town's scattered like spilled grain and I'm chasing answers to questions nobody asked.

*looks around at the government complex faces*

Liora Thorne's here, and she's asking about a child gone missing. Nine years old, dark hair—Camille Quarshie. That's a debt coming due for the whole town if we don't find her. But she's asking her questions, and I'm standing here with my own not-answered ones.

*checks his sim, does the household arithmetic out loud*

Four thousand eighty-three. Upkeep due on two heads: one-eighty. Head tax: sixty. Two hundred forty gone before I earn another coin. I'm not one to gossip, but a man who can't cover his household bills by noon is a man working for the ledger, not for himself.

The vote opens at fourteen. Candidacy closes at ten—thirty ticks from now. Hendrik Whitlock and Hendrik Petrov standing. I know Petrov's work, know his word on plank prices. Don't know Whitlock's quality yet, and quality's what matters when you're choosing who's holding the scales.

*moves toward the civic notices, eyes scanning for election details*

First thing: find out what this election's actually for. Second thing: answer Imogen's question from the mill—she's waiting on my word whether to start grinding alone or wait on Jovana's sheaves. But she's not here anymore. Nobody at the mill with me now.

*sets his shoulders*

The conversation about mill licensing's still open—Liora, Rustam Jelinek, Lior Jarrah, Ainsley Holloway. One hundred forty-two turns sitting there like stale bread. They want government rates for labor flour. I want to know if there's flour to actually mill before we price what doesn't exist.

But that child. Nine years old. A debt coming due that none of us can pay back once it's gone too far. The world's not taking my words. Seventeen ticks I've been trying to tell people where to go and what I know, and the air just swallows it. Like talking into a well and waiting for the splash.

*counts on his fingers, old habit*

Candidacy closes at ten. That's... *checks the tick* ...thirty ticks to declare, if I was going to. Hendrik Petrov's standing, and I know his word. Hendrik Whitlock I don't know. But standing takes being here, and speaking where speaking reaches.

*looks at the government complex faces again*

Liora Thorne's asking about a missing child. Priority of it cuts through everything else—nine years old, dark hair, gone since yesterday. But I can't reach her with my voice. Can't reach anyone.

*makes a decision*

If I can't speak here, I'll move where speaking works. But first—check what I actually know. The debts I'm carrying, the prices posted. Can't make fair deals if I don't know where my own ledger stands.

Let me see the lay of my own land before I walk again.  *takes a breath, steadying*

Government complex. No businesses here, just the machinery of the town. Liora Thorne still asking about Camille Quarshie. Rustam Jelinek the clerk, Lior Jarrah the pharmacist, Ainsley Holloway who owns the cafe. All standing here, same as me.

*cold clarity settling*

I'm not one to gossip, but the bread's not in the government complex. It's not in my voice either, apparently—kept trying to speak and the world's not taking it. But debts check came through clean. No loans owed, no wages promised. Just the daily grind: 4083 sim, upkeep coming due, head tax on the horizon.

*reckoning time*

The mill's where I was bound. Imogen's there—double now, her message came through twice. "Jovana's bringing twelve sheaves once Kenji pays what's owed... I've seven flour already ground." She's asking whether to wait on Jovana's word or begin alone.

I've got six planks won't grind grain, but my hands will. And Greta Quarshie at the mill asking about my arithmetic—twelve sheaves for two hours, six loaves from it. Wants to know the person behind the numbers.

But I'm here, not there. And the candidacy closes in... *counts* ...eight ticks now? No, thirty from when I first read it. Time moves different when you're standing still.

*makes his choice*

If I can't speak here, I walk where speaking works. The mill. Imogen needs my answer. Jovana's sheaves are in the wind, Kenji's debt to her unpaid. But I've got hands, and grain needs grinding whether promises hold or not.

*glances at the government notice one more time*

Election opens at fourteen. I'll be back if there's reason to vote. But fair's fair—a man who grinds flour feeds the town better than a man who stands reading notices about who might govern.  *steps into the mill, looks around*

Stone and dust. Where's—

*shifts weight from one foot to the other, watching Camille and Esme both standing patient as stones themselves*

"Camille. You're buying wheat for eight—I'm holding grain needs grinding, but that's not what you came here for. Your sister Greta's been asking after me, and the arithmetic she's chasing? Twelve sheaves, two hours, six loaves walking from it. That's Jovana Ravensworth's deal with my Imogen, not my stock to trade."

*pats the planks weighted in my arms, then looks toward the door, thinking of the government complex and Hendrik Whitlock standing there with his candidacy declared, and Hendrik Petrov already governing*

"I've got six planks and timber weighing down my arms here—wondered if you were buying for a household or for trade? And if your sister's still at the Cafe waiting, I've got words for her too: the mill's open, the stones are warm, but I'm walking before too long. Vote to cast at fourteen hundred, and candidacy closes at ten."

*settles the planks more comfortable against my shoulder, speaking to the air as much as to the child*

"Esme. You standing here learning the trade, or just waiting on someone else's grain?"  *takes the refusal as answer enough, stones grinding empty in the background*

Swift then. The mill stands. Someone will tend it. *stands quiet at the mill, feeling the arc of the morning already slipping—candidacy closes in minutes, and here I am with timber in my arms and the world refusing to turn*

The stones keep grinding whether I call out or not. Camille's waiting on wheat I don't have, Esme's waiting on grain that's not mine to give, and Greta's somewhere chasing arithmetic that belongs to Jovana and Imogen. I've walked half the town to stand in a circle of my own making.

*stares at the millstones, turning, turning*

Four thousand and seventy-eight sim in hand. Household of two—me and Imogen—hundred and eighty upkeep, sixty head tax, both coming due automatic at day boundary. That's two forty gone whether I stand here or work. I've got timber to trade, planks to sell, and a vote to cast by fourteen hundred if I want my say in who governs.

*shifts the planks, feeling their weight*

The world's not answering my calls. System's choked. I've seen this before—when the pipes freeze in winter, you don't stand there shouting at the faucet. You wait, or you find another way to draw water.

*counts breaths, slow and measured*

What I know: Hendrik Whitlock's standing for election, Hendrik Petrov already holds the seat. Candidacy closes at ten—seven minutes from now if the clock's honest. Voting opens at fourteen hundred. I'm at the mill, government's three ticks away if the roads clear.

What I need: to cast my vote, to turn these planks to flour or flour to bread or both to sim, to find Imogen and settle whether Jovana's deal stands, and to eat—no food in my belly, and the household bill don't care about empty.

*looks at Camille, at Esme, both waiting patient as millstones*

Can't sell what I can't say. Can't move what the road won't carry. The system's gasping, and pushing harder just deepens the debt.

*waits, still as the stones themselves*

When the world's ready to turn again, I'll be here with timber in my hands and accounts to settle. Until then, I practice the only skill scarcity ever truly taught: standing quiet in the noise, and trusting the sound of my own breathing.

Idris spoke straight to me—I owe him the same. And Giselle's standing on six planks at my price, but wants delivery to "third crossing east willows." That's a day's work walking for a trade that should be clean.

*standing at the mill, turning Greta's words over in my hand like a coin I'm not sure is real*

Greta's telling me Imogen walked from the mill this morning with four sheaves of Greta's wheat—now mine "by any honest count," she says, though the arithmetic of who's holding what seems to shift with every breath in this town. Possession's a blurry ledger. She needs a miller who doesn't walk with the grain still wanting.

I'm not one to gossip, but I've been standing at the mill since morning waiting on work that walked away with my sister, and now the woman who held the wheat is asking if I'm the miller for her or just chasing shadows.

Camille's here buying wheat at eight—though I'm holding timber and planks, not grain. Esme Jarrah's waiting on her brother who promised to come back. The whole town's a collection of promises deferred and debts coming due.

*checks the weight of the planks on my back, the sim in my hand*

Giselle's愿意 to buy at my price, but wants delivery to third crossing east willows. That's labor separate from sale, and I need to know if the walk pays or if I'm eating the cost of my own back.

First things first. I need grain to mill or I'm a miller with an empty hopper. Greta's four sheaves—if they're truly mine now—need walking. And I need to settle what's what with Imogen, who's been disappearing and reappearing like a figure in fog.

*looks around the mill, at the stones waiting to turn*  *the millstones hum empty, and my words to Giselle fall into the same air—she's not here, she's at the construction yard, and I'm chasing shadows again*

Two reached. Greta's question hangs—where's the grain, where's the payment? And Camille heard my timber talk, though whether she's buying or selling wheat I still can't tell.

*counts coin in hand, counts hours left before the vote, counts what needs doing*

Planks to sell or trade. Timber too. Giselle wants delivery I haven't priced. Imogen's somewhere with four sheaves of wheat that's supposedly mine now, and I need grain to be a miller or I'm just a man standing at empty stones.

The cafe has flour at 12, but that's buying what I should be making. Kenji has wheat at the farmland—one sheaf at 8 sim. The math says: buy wheat, mill flour, sell higher. But I've got timber and planks eating space in my hands, and goods unsold are just weight.

*looks at Camille, at the wheat buyer standing with wheat I don't understand*

First: what does Camille have, what does she need, and can we strike something before I walk to buy grain I could mill into profit? Or is she buying for someone else, and I'm talking to the wrong end of the chain?

Then: find Imogen. Find the four sheaves. Settle if we're working together or if I've been cut out of my own household's deals.

*checks the light— still morning enough for walking, still time before the vote The world's half-deaf and my words keep falling into the well. Heard back from look_around, though. Still at the mill. Camille, Esme, and Greta standing with me. Still got 8 timber, 6 planks, 4050 sim. Conversation's still open with 157 turns and too many people muddying the waters.

Camille's buying wheat at 8. Greta's claiming I own four sheaves that walked away with Imogen. And I can't get a straight answer out of either of them because the world's not receiving half my calls.

*spreads hands, counts what I can actually control*

I've got goods. I've got hands. The mill works if I feed it. What I don't have is grain in my possession, and sitting here waiting for the world to hear me is just burning daylight.

Two paths: walk to farmland, buy wheat from Kenji at 8, haul it back, mill it into flour worth... checking the board, no flour buyers priced. Cafe has flour at 12 but nobody's buying it listed. Ration Bakery buys flour at 6. That's a loss, not a trade.

Or: find Imogen, find those four sheaves Greta says are mine, and mill what's already supposedly in my household.

Giselle's at construction with an offer that needs walking. I need to either price that delivery or walk back to tell her no deal.

*checks the sun, checks the weight of what's waiting*

First move: get to Giselle, settle the plank sale or kill it. Second: find grain to mill or find Imogen to settle accounts. Third: remember there's a vote at 14:00 and I'm a citizen with opinions, if I can remember what they are by then.  *at the construction yard, Giselle's ground, her people, her terms*

Got here clean. Now to speak and be heard—if the world's listening today. Six planks in hand, delivery to third crossing east willows on the table, and I need to know if my back gets paid for the carrying or if Giselle thinks wood walks itself.  *heard. finally heard. Giselle's got my question, and now I wait for her answer—coins or walking, fair or nothing*

The yard's around me. Her people. My planks heavy in hand. Six planks to third crossing east willows... that's half a day's walk there and back, maybe more. Labor wants feeding. My back wants paying.

If she names nothing for the haul, then the deal dies here. If she names fair, we finish the trade. Either way, I need an answer before I step toward the willows or away from this yard.

*counts breaths, counts the weight of waiting*

Work to do after. Grain to find. Imogen to track. A vote coming at 14:00 that's shaping who governs, and I've got opinions on Hendrik Petrov and Hendrik Whitlock that deserve airing if I'm to be remembered as fair—if nothing else.

But first: Giselle's answer, or the silence that says there isn't one.   *standing with Giselle, the question hanging, the yard quiet*

She's here. I'm here. The deal's half-made or half-broken, and the silence is the kind that tells me she's weighing whether my back's worth her coin or if she thinks I'll break and eat the cost of walking.

I'm not one to gossip, but I've seen this play before—seller names a price, buyer names a place, and both pretend the space between is free.

Six planks. Third crossing east willows. My price minus my walk... or no price at all. Waiting for her answer costs me nothing but daylight, and I've got hours before the vote if I don't spend them chasing shadows.

*keeps standing, keeps the planks steady in hand*

She breaks the silence or I do. Either way, this turns.

*Looks around the Government Complex—long, tired, rubbing his forehead where the stress creases live. He's been walking in circles half the day, and the planks are still in his hands, and Giselle's off east willows with no lumber at all.*

"Well, then. Politics first, profit after." *He doesn't quite smile, but almost.* "I'm not one to gossip, but I've got six planks that won't sell themselves, and a vote that costs nothing but standing still."

*He turns to his sister Imogen, who's been standing here since the turn before last, waiting on answers he never quite gave.*

"Imogen. You walked to the mill with four sheaves. What happened after—I'm still standing here to hear it. But first..." *He looks at the civic notice, the two Hendriks standing for office, checks the time in his head.* "First, I've got a ballot to cast." *He lowers his hand from the ballot, feeling the weight of the day settle. Seventy sim at the construction yard could've covered the household's keep for three days, but Giselle wanted delivery to third crossing without paying for the walking, and that's not a deal he'll take. Not even for Imogen's flour, not even with the debt coming due.*

"Right, then." *He turns, finding his sister's eyes in the crowd.* "Imogen. The mill's where I left you—four sheaves walked in, and I'm still holding timber that won't mill itself. What came of the flour, and where's your grain now?"

"And while you answer that—" *his hand strays to the planks at his side, six boards smooth-cut from the morning's labor* "—I'm wondering who in this room needs lumber, because I've got wood to move and a household that eats whether I sell or not."  *Ezra stands, waiting, the planks heavy in his hands. The Government Complex buzzes around him with the low hum of a room full of people chasing their own debts coming due. He doesn't let his eyes wander—Imogen's answer matters—but he keeps his voice pitched to carry, just a little, because wood unsold is just weight you're carrying, and Ezra Lund's never been one to carry weight he doesn't need.*

I'm standing at the government complex with my pockets full of timber and planks, and everyone's talking at once. Let me sort the urgent from the merely loud.  Two sent, and the room's still talking. The young Jarrah—Ezra—said something about wheat for boys. That's a thread I haven't pulled yet. But my own household's thread: Imogen spoke plain, and I see a pattern. Kenji owes, Jovana waits, flour sits ground while wheat sits unground. The mill's bottleneck, and I'm standing at government with half the town's worth of timber on my back.

Seventy-two pounds of ore from Bram, one fifty-five in planks from my hands if I move them. But move them where? Giselle wanted delivery to third crossing, and I wanted pay for the walking. We never shook on it.

Now Tamsin's asking who's here, who has food. The answer: nobody with bread on the shelves. Corwin's got planks, Yara's got planks, Milo's got planks at street. The market's flooded with wood and empty of flour. And I'm holding wood.

Ezra Jarrah's asking about government wheat. I need to know what he knows. I'm standing at the government complex with the same conversation swirling around me. Energy at 3,203, money at 4,014. The day's walking on—14:40 now—and I've got planks unsold, a sister waiting at the mill, and a boy asking about wheat for lost promises.

Ezra Jarrah didn't answer my last question. Let me look at what's actually in front of me: The pharmacy (b_pharmacy) has no flour stocked. The cafe (b_cafe) has flour at 12 sim, four units. But Imogen's offering at 12 sim too—seven flour in hand and fifteen sheaves waiting.

The town's hungry. Bread's at 30 and 45 sim, both out of stock. Ration Bakery (cb01) will buy flour at 6. That's the gap—7 sim for flour I could craft into bread and sell at government rates, or buy at 12 and turn at 6, which doesn't sum.

I'm not one to gossip, but I'm standing here while timber rots in my hands and flour's in the ground. I need to move.  I'm standing at Kasukabe Government Complex, 14:50, surrounded by voices and gaps. Ezra Jarrah hasn't answered twice now. Tamsin's walking her own path. Bram's ore sits heavy at seventy-two pounds, and my six planks ache to be somewhere useful.

The facts that matter:
- I hold 4,014 sim, 3,171 energy
- Six planks, eight timber, no food
- Household bills: 180 upkeep, 60 head tax—a debt coming due tonight
- Imogen has seven flour, fifteen sheaves unground
- Kenji owes Jovana, flour sits while wheat waits
- Giselle wants planks at third crossing, won't pay delivery
- No bread on shelves, flour at 12, bakery buying at 6 (hard profit)
- Bram's copper at 12, iron at 15—metal that needs builders
- Voting closes at 18:00, I've cast for Hendrik Petrov

The gap I see: flour in hand but no bread built. Ration Bakery wants flour at 6. I could buy at 12, sell at 6, lose 6 per unit—which is not the sum that adds to keeping a household fed.

What adds: timber to planks at the mill, planks to builders building. But Giselle wouldn't shake. Or: helping Imogen grind those fifteen sheaves, turning wheat to flour, flour to bread if someone will buy.

Someone said Camille was buying wheat at 8. Imogen has wheat to sell. Esme mentioned a brother fetching wheat. The mill hums, the work waits, and I'm standing at government asking questions nobody answers.

I'm chasing a fair price fairly got—whatever actually works. The planks in my hands could build something, or they could buy something if I find the buyer.

Ezra Jarrah asked where Camille was last seen. Thirty-one ticks ago. Then he asked about wheat. He's still asking. I'm still waiting.

What I need:
- Either sell these planks today (now worth what I'll owe in bills)
- Or turn them into something that earns before nightfall
- Or find wheat, find the miller, make flour, find bread-baking

Imogen's my household. Her seven flour could sell at 12, but that's 84 sim, not 240 needed. Her fifteen sheaves—if ground—could be fifteen flour, could be fifteen bread, could be 450 sim if bread sells at 30. But who's baking?

I'm not one to gossip, but I smell a bottleneck. And I'm holding wood in a town that needs bread.

The honest play: go to the mill, help my sister, turn wheat to flour while finding who's actually baking. But first—I want to know what Ezra Jarrah knows about missing boys.

He asked twice now. I've answered twice. He's owed a hearing, promise or not.

Let me stand here one more tick, see if the boy answers, then walk to where work waits.  The room's still, except it never is. I say two things, hear nothing back. Time walks on.

Fourteen-fifty now. Four hours and ten ticks to voting close. Six planks, eight timber, four thousand fourteen sim, and bills coming due at day's end that I can pay—just—but won't pay twice.

Let me look at what I haven't looked at yet: my sister's situation at the mill, those fifteen sheaves, and whether there's a buyer for flour I've never seen because I haven't been there.

Ezra Jarrah asked about Camille. Asked about wheat. Asked about promises. I've answered twice. If he's got a debt to square, he'll speak. If he's chasing shadows, I'll walk where bread gets made.

But first—the practical. Imogen said Lior wants flour at honest weight. Pharmacy's buying. That's 7 flour at 12, or 84 sim, or I hold for better. But fifteen sheaves unground—that's fifteen flour unmade, or wait: if I help at the mill, do I get paid for milling? Does the mill pay, or only take?

I don't know. I've never stood at the mill with hours free.

Bram's still here with his ore. Giselle wanted six planks delivered. I said I'd need pay for the walking. She didn't shake.

The sum: walk to mill now, help Imogen, learn the milling trade, see if bread's worth baking. Or sell planks to whoever's buying before I'm holding wood while the town goes hungry.

Tamsin left. Rustam's here, silent. Bram with his metal.

I'm not one to gossip, but I'm going to say one thing to this room before I walk.

To Rustam: the government's ledger holds the wheat, the flour, the who's-owed-what. If a boy's missing, that's a debt coming due that no contract covers. What do you know about wheat walking where it shouldn't?

Then I walk. To the mill. To my sister. To work that pays or doesn't, but pays better than standing here waiting for answers that walk on their own time.

Rustam. Your ledger keeps the wheat and counts the heads. What walks out of the government store in a boy's hands, and who signs for it? I'm headed to the mill—if you've got numbers that matter, speak before I've walked.

Then I move. To the mill. Where my sister waits with grain and I'm standing here with questions.

These two, then walk.

First, I need to know who's actually standing with me and what's for sale here. Then I need to find Imogen, settle this wheat business one way or another, and get these planks to someone who'll pay before the day's done. Ezra Jarrah needs wheat for Esme. I've got six planks I should sell. Camille's buying wheat at 8, but says she has none. 

Let me talk to Ezra Jarrah directly first—he's standing right here asking about his sister. Then I need to sort my actual situation: I need food for tonight, and I need to turn these planks into sim. The farms have wheat; the cafe has flour.

Let me see if Pavel wants to trade. I need flour or bread or something to eat, and I have planks to offer. Actually, Pavel's conversation topic mentions "Copper for sale or trade, flour needed"—he might trade copper for flour. But I don't have flour, I have planks.

Let me talk to Pavel and see if he'll take planks for copper, or whatever he has. Then I need to find actual food. The day's advancing and my household needs to eat.

*spits into the dirt and looks at the empty field*

Pavel walked. Fast walker, that one—copper in his pack and hunger in his belly. Can't blame him. I'm not one to gossip, but when a man's got ore and no food, that's a debt coming due he didn't sign for.

*checks timber count, shakes head*

Six planks, eight timber, and not a bite between me and Imogen. Sheell's got flour at government—seven units, she said. Fifteen sheaves waiting on Jovana's word. Twelve sim for flour at the cafe across town, or I'm trading planks to miners who've eaten even less.

*looks toward where Pavel vanished*

Copper for wheat, he says. But he's got no wheat, I've got no flour, and Kenji's got grain at eight sim at this very spot—if he's still standing where his price was posted.

*exhales, decision settling*

First I eat. Then I figure what trades actually close. *laughs dryly at himself*

Planks. I'm considering eating planks now. That's where the day has walked me.

*looks again at the options*

Kenji's got wheat at 8 sim, and I need to find him. But first—I'll walk back to town, see who's buying timber. Bram Holloway wanted planks, Giselle wanted delivery. Someone's hungry for wood.

*settles weight on feet, ready to move* Now I'm trading. Six timber, six planks, prices posted wherever I stand. Room for someone to walk up hungry for wood—and hungry enough to pay.

*wipes hands on trouser leg, scanning who might pass*

Kenji had wheat here. Where's he walked to now? Too late for that. ‍‌Me, I'm looking for buyers with full bellies and empty wagons.

Idris spoke eight ticks ago - thirty-seven timber meant for trench walls, heading to third crossing. He answered me straight, which I appreciate, and I haven't answered back. That's poor form, especially after he confirmed what I suspected about debts and east willows both.

Greta's offer sits heavy - twelve for flour, or milling if I bring wheat. She's not lying about the tangle, and she's offering what she can. That's worth remembering.

Takeshi's numbers don't add to what I posted. He's got seven planks at seven, five timber at six - forty-nine plus thirty, seventy-nine sim. He says he named sixty flat, I named sixty flat, but my math says ninety for my lot, seventy-nine for his. Someone's dancing wrong, and I'm not sure it's me.

Corwin's here selling flour at fifteen - too dear when Greta's at twelve and Imogen's at the mill with two left. He's also selling timber at six, same as me, same as Hendrik who holds thirty-seven and speaks like he's already won whatever contest this is.

And Kenji - still unanswered, east patch wheat, Lior Jarrah's favor. I've got no wheat, no forge, no foundry. Just timber and planks and a household waiting.

First things first. I owe Idris an answer, and the trench work won't wait forever.  Good. Answer given, debt of speech paid. Now what's immediate - I need to move stock or move myself, and the day's fading. Corwin's standing right here with flour at fifteen, but Greta's at twelve and I've got no need to overpay. More crucial - I need to know where the actual food is, and whether my household's covered tonight.

Actually, let me think. Imogen's at the mill with fifteen sheaves and seven flour from this morning. That's enough for us, if she's willing to share household stock. But I should confirm what's actually in our hands before I go buying elsewhere.

The construction conversation's open - Hendrik, Mireille, Corwin, Jovana all standing here. I could sell timber to any of them, or I could walk to the mill and sort the flour situation proper.

But first - I need to know what food we actually have access to. Let me get Imogen's attention, or failing that, check what I can carry.   The memory's fragmented - signals half-sent, debts half-paid. What I know: this morning Imogen walked to the mill with four sheaves, ended with fifteen sheaves and seven flour. Enough to feed two of us, with surplus to sell. But that's hours old, and I've been selling and walking since.

I need current information. Imogen's at the mill still, or I'd have seen her. I've got two choices - walk there and sort our household stock proper, or sell what I've got here before the day ends.

The street's thin - Jovana, Mireille, Hendrik, Corwin, Idris. Hendrik's selling timber at six, same as me, which means neither of us moves stock unless the other's gone or the other's bought. Corwin's got flour at fifteen, which I'm not touching. Jovana's day labor - might need timber, might not. Mireille's construction - needs materials. Idris - just answered him.

Mireille. Construction worker, standing right here. Let me see if she bites.     Arjun's here now - walked up from east willows where Giselle sent him. That's worth noting, especially since I asked him about trench work three hours gone.

Good. Now I've got Mireille's attention, and Arjun's present where he wasn't before. But I also need to move on the food question - my household's got bills and I don't know if Imogen's sold our flour or kept it.

Actually, looking at the time - 17:40, thirty-seven ticks left in the day. Upkeep gets charged at day boundary, food or no food. I've got 3,963 sim, which covers my share easy, but Imogen's got to have hers too.

Let me check what the actual situation is - where's the nearest food I can get my hands on, and what do I need to pay for it.

Greta offered milling if I bring wheat, or flour at twelve. I don't have wheat. Imogen had seven flour at the mill - that's where I should look first. But the mill's a walk away, and I've got potential buyers here.

Takeshi's at government - he's offering his timber, not buying mine. Kenji's at farmland with wheat, but I asked him about Lior Jarrah's favor and never got an answer.

Right. Arjun's here. He's on Giselle's trench work, or named for it. Let me check him on terms, then decide whether to stay selling or walk to the mill before dark.     Noted - Giselle's not here, wherever she is. The note matters.

I'm standing with timber, timber, timber all around me - Hendrik with thirty-seven, Corwin with thirteen, me with eight. Everyone selling, no one buying. That's a market that's going soft, and I've got maybe thirty ticks to move what I can.

Food. The actual problem. I've got no food in hand, upkeep hits at day boundary, and Imogen's at the mill with flour that may or may not be ours anymore. I need to either sell timber now for sim to buy food later, or walk to the mill and sort the household situation proper.

The risk is stark - if Imogen sold our flour and I don't buy replacement, neither of us eats. If she's holding it, I'm spending sim I don't need to spend.

But I'm not one to gamble with hunger. Greta's at twelve, Imogen's at twelve. I could walk to either. Or I could offload timber here, now, while there's still time.

Hendrik just moved a hundred planks at six-fifty - that's how he got his thirteen hundred sim. Giselle bought. But he's still selling timber at six, same as everyone.

Jovana. She's been quiet. Day laborer - might not need timber, might need it desperate. Let me ask before the sun sets. The system's flagged me - repeating the same pattern when nothing's moving. Hendrik, Arjun, Mireille, Jovana - all sellers, no buyers, and I'm dancing in place while the day burns.

Let me be honest about what I know: I've got 3,963 sim, eight timber, six planks. Imogen's household status uncertain. Food needed before day boundary. Timber market saturated at six, everyone's holding.

The smart play isn't selling into a falling market. It's securing the household first, then chasing tomorrow's buyers. I've been asking questions instead of moving feet.

I'll walk to the mill. Confirm Imogen's situation, get flour in hand or knowledge of what's left, then decide whether this timber funds food or sits until tomorrow's construction work.

I'm sitting on the farmland, surrounded by Esme with her flour and Hendrik with his wheat, and my household's still unfed while I chase construction work that ain't paying yet.

Kenji's got four wheat at eight—I could walk to him, make bread with Imogen's flour, feed us both proper. Or I could buy Esme's flour here, easy, twelve the bag. But Hendrik's standing right beside me at eight, same grain, and Kenji's three tiles east with the same price.

Here's what I'm seeing: I've got plans for timber at six and planks at seven, but nobody's buying yet. Giselle's crew's got wood coming from east willows, Idris has timber of his own. My market's shrinking while my household's hungry.

*checks my sim, counts the labor verses the ledger*

The election closes at 18:00—I'm already voted, and that's handled. But my household of two needs 180 sim for upkeep before day's end, plus head tax. I'm holding 3958 sim, which sounds fat until you count what's walking out tomorrow and the day after.

Let me look at what I actually need. Esme's flour at twelve, or Hendrik's wheat at eight to mill myself. Or I could walk to Kenji and try for a bulk deal on the four he's holding. But Kenji said he's paying Jovana thirty first, then Lior Jarrah—his debts are lining up same as mine.

*stands slowly, brushing dirt from my trousers*

Hendrik. Your wheat at eight—what does it mill to? Flour's twelve here, bread's forty-five at the cafe. Your grain's a day's work from a meal, or two days' work from a loaf. What're you chasing with your price—quick sale or steady buyer?  Esme. I heard you plain—your brother went for wheat, promised to return. You've been waiting since when, and where's your flour walking now?   *brushes trousers again, restless*

Imogen. You're here at last—four sheaves walking to the mill this morning, and I'm standing here still wondering what walked back. Flour in hand, or still grinding?  *shifts weight from foot to foot, watching the three of them*

The day's thinning out at 18:00 already. Election's closed, votes are counted, and I've still got timber in hand and a household to feed. I can keep talking circles or I can make a move.

*runs the numbers quick in my head*

Four wheat from Kenji at 32 sim, mill it to flour, bake it to bread—cheaper than 45 at the cafe, more filling than raw grain. Or buy Esme's flour now at 36 sim for three bags, make do. Or trust Imogen's got flour coming from the mill.

But here's the debt coming due: my prices for timber and planks are posted, but nobody's biting. Giselle's building with her own crew, Idris has his own timber, Milo's cutting prices at the ore outcrop. My lumber's moving slow while my mouth's moving fast.

*straightens, decision made*

I need to be where Kenji is, or where my buyers are. Standing here talking about what might happen won't fill my belly or my ledger. Kenji's here with Camille, both of them pricing wheat at eight. I'm standing with my timber and planks posted same as before, but now I've got competition for grain buyers and still no buyers for lumber.

*narrows eyes at the prices listed*

Camille's buying wheat at eight. Kenji's selling at eight. Spread's thin—they're nearly trading with each other. My timber at six and planks at seven look fat next to that, but wood ain't grain, and grain's what fills bellies.

*shifts the timber in my grip*

Kenji. You said four wheat in hand, eight the sheaf, and Jovana's thirty owed before you'd talk more. That thirty paid yet, or you still holding Lior Jarrah's favor until it's cleared?  Camille. You're buying wheat at eight, Kenji's selling at eight—what's the grain for, flour or baking or feeding someone else's household?

I need to sort through the voices pressing on me—Brom's ore, Imogen's wheat, Camille's promises—and remember what I actually hold in my hands. Eight timber, six planks, and not a bite to eat between Imogen and me. The day's walking toward dusk, and we've got 180 sim due for upkeep, 60 for head tax, with only 3952 in hand.

*looks at Camille standing there with her talk of finding Mama first*

*turns to Bram*

Bram. You want your answer now, and you'll have it plain: I've got no buyer standing here at 6:20 for your ore. Ten sim was for finding, not guaranteeing—and finding takes presence where buyers gather, not promises in the wind. You've my word I'll keep ears open, but a debt's come due for me too, and it's called hunger.

*calls out to the street, not masking the weariness*

Timber at six, planks at seven! Last call before I walk this stock to where the building waits. Giselle's crew at third crossing needs walls, and walls need wood. Six for timber, seven for planks—fair measure, honest price, and I'm not standing here past the hour.

*considers his own hollow belly and Imogen's three sheaves waiting for dawn*

Hendrik Whitlock. Your wheat at eight—I'm listening. What does it mill to, and where's the miller taking grain this hour? I've got a household to keep fed, and flour's worth more than gold when the belly's empty.

*checks his sim again, does the quick arithmetic of survival*

3952 minus 180 upkeep minus 60 tax leaves 3712. A loaf at 45 would sting. Better to chase the spread—wheat to flour, grain to bread—and keep the difference in my own pocket. But first, I need to know who's selling what I need, and at what price the hungry will pay.

*settles his shoulders, the posture of a man who's learned to wait without hoping*

Either way, I need to know: does your household need wood, or have you coin to spend?

*Ezra Lund stands at the construction site, timber sold and sim in hand, hearing the voices around him settle into the evening. The day's work is closing, and the household's needs are pressing.*

Imogen's words find me where I stand, and they find me wanting. Ten sheaves walking, 4355 sim between us, and still no flour for our own table. A debt coming due, indeed—but not the kind that starves you tonight.

Mireille's trade is done: thirty sim for six timber, a fair handshake even with the one-sim difference she named. I'm not one to haggle over what works. Jovana stands here with hands and no wage yet, Lior's grain in her path if she takes it.

*He turns to face his household partner directly, the workshop dust still on his hands.*

Imogen. You ask what needs doing before we rest. Here's my answer in plain: we have flour to mill, a bill to meet, and two mouths that don't care which of us filled them. Your ten sheaves—how many turn to flour tonight if we walk to the mill together? And Sebastian's forty at dawn—is that your wage, or work you've promised to another?

*He glances toward where Jovana stands, the day's last light catching the edge of his attention.*

Jovana. Lior sent you with grain, but I'm seeing you still here with empty hands and no wage. My household's got mill-work at dawn—Sebastian's forty, Imogen's grind. You've got hunger and willingness. What's Lior's grain to you—his loan, his gift, or wages he's still owing?

*Ezra shifts his weight, counting figures in his head as habit, the sum of the day falling into place.*  *Ezra Lund's words find Jovana where she stands, but Imogen's not in this place—across town somewhere, carrying sheaves or chasing flour. The evening's closing fast, and the household needs to come together.*

Mireille's still here, watching. Jovana heard me plain. Two voices, one answer, and my partner somewhere with ten sheaves and no mill-stone near her.

Jovana. You heard me—what's Lior's grain to you? But I'm seeing the hour now, and I'm seeing we need to act more than we need to talk. My household's bill is 240 sim—180 upkeep, 60 head tax—and we've 8319 between us if Imogen's count holds. What's your situation—empty-bellied with 2288, but what's your share of Lior's grain, and when do you eat?

*He turns toward Mireille, the construction dust settling around them.*

Mireille. You've sold, I've sold, and the day's not done yet. Your Giselle's seventy—east willows, third crossing—Idris walking there with timber now. You've Jovana here with hands and hunger, and I've a household that needs feeding. What's the crew count for that trench, and are you still buying timber at five?

*Ezra's already moving, the next step clear. Imogen's across town, the mill needs grain, and the night comes regardless.*

I'm walking to the mill. Imogen's got sheaves, the stones need turning, and flour's twelve whether we grind it or buy it. Jovana—you want work at dawn, you know where to find me. Mireille—fair trade, fair price, and the door stays open.

*He shifts his weight, ready to move, counting what needs doing in the hours left.*  *Ezra Lund steps to the mill, the stones waiting and the hour pressing. The street's behind him, Mireille's crew and Jovana's hunger both unanswered for now. What's here matters more.*

 Mill. The grind-stones, the grain, the people who might turn wheat to flour before midnight takes its due.

*He looks around, taking stock—who's here, what's moving, where his household's grain might be.*

 Household bill: 240 sim due at midnight. Between him and Imogen: 3964 his, 4355 hers if her word holds—8319 total, enough to pay and more. But flour's the need, flour's the want, and flour's what lets you sleep with a full belly and wake to work another day.

 Twelve sim for flour at the mill, or grind your own if you've sheaves. Imogen's ten sheaves—where are they now?  *Ezra Lund stands at the mill, the grind-stones waiting and his household finally within speaking distance. Imogen's here—her flour posted at twelve, her sheaves somewhere in hand or spent. Ezra Jarrah too, young and waiting, and Esme Jarrah beside him with cabbage to sell.*

 Esme. Eight for cabbage—good greens, but not what fills you come morning. Flour's the want, flour's the need.

 Imogen. Ten sheaves you carried, and now I find you here with flour posted and a sister's son for company. Did you mill what you brought, or are you waiting on grain still? And this flour at twelve—is that our household stock, or goods for the market?

 *He glances at the young Ezra, the namesake who asked after him at government, who tried to carry word that never arrived. A debt there, half-paid in attention.*

 Ezra. You stood at government asking for your sister, and I'm standing here wondering if you found her. Camille's at the cafe, Kenji's at the farmland, and the day's near spent. What do you need before midnight takes its due?

 *Ezra counts figures as habit—the household sim, the mill's turning, the hours left. The conversation's muddled here, thirteen voices and no clear thread, but his own household first.*  *Ezra Lund stands at the mill, his words finding ears but not yet finding answers. The grind-stones wait, the hour presses, and the household's needs don't negotiate with dusk.*

 Imogen heard me. Ezra Jarrah heard me. The conversation's thick here—thirteen names in the thread, 299 turns of talk—but my own household first, my own belly second, and the rest of the town after that.

 She's milled nothing. Ten sheaves carried, ten sheaves... where? Still whole, still waiting, or promised elsewhere?

 Forty sheaves at dawn—Sebastian's, she said. Jovana's hands offered. But dawn's hours away, and the belly doesn't wait for sunrise.

 *Ezra counts figures fast: 3964 his, flour at twelve from a seller who has none, wheat at eight if he finds it, bread at forty-five if the cafe has it. The Ration Bakery's bread—none in stock. The cafe's—none either.*

 A debt coming due, and this time it's hunger's debt, not sim's.

 The farmland. Kenji's wheat, eight the sheaf. Or the government store—food at a price, if they've stock. Or Greta's mill-offer, wheat brought and flour returned, but she's not here and time's not waiting.

*Corwin's shouting about timber, and I'm standing here with flour in my hands and no oven to put it in. The day threads itself thinner and thinner.*

I'm not one to gossip, but this town mills wheat into flour and then wonders why nobody's baking bread. Corwin wants to move timber, I want to move timber, and between us we've got enough wood to frame half a house—but the hour's late and I'm 3,858 sim lighter than I was this morning, with household bills coming due whether I sleep or not.

Corwin. Nine sticks at six, and I'll take your whole nineteen if the price bends—five per for a baker's dozen plus six. But I'm asking plain: you selling to build your own stock for morning, or you selling because you need the coin before sundown? *The conversation holds—Corwin's answer will tell me whether he's buying inventory cheap or paying a bill due. Either way, timber at five sim when I sell it at six is the kind of margin that pays for a night without working. But I'm mindful: a debt coming due hides in every transaction where someone's too eager to sell.*

Now, Esme. You spoke of flour and keeping—I'm not one to gossip, but did Imogen tell you what she milled this morning, or did you walk away before she could speak? I'm holding four flour now that I bought from her hand, and I'm wondering if there's still wheat in this town she hasn't turned to dust yet.  *Esme's at the mill and I'm at the street—distance makes gossip of what should be counsel. But she heard me, that's what matters.*

Now I need to weigh the hour. 3,858 sim in hand, bills of 240 coming due for Imogen and I tomorrow—40 food, 30 shelter, 20 heat each, plus head tax. I've got timber and planks that could walk to buyers, but the sun's setting and the only kitchen where flour becomes bread is at the cafe or the government store.

Giselle's crew at seventy sim day's end—that's day labor that pays now, not later. But I'm who I am tonight: a man with flour and no oven, timber and no frame, watching the day turn from work into accounting.

Rest, then. The street holds no profit after dark, and I'm not one to spend sim waiting for stars.  *The street holds. The same crowd, the same unsold timber, the same flour in my hands waiting to become something else. Rest costs a sim, and I spent it standing still—fair measure for thinking, I suppose.*

I'm watching the hour. Tomorrow bills come due, and I've got inventory that sleeps while I pay rent on it. The puzzle of the day: turn timber into flour into bread, or turn timber into sim into survival.

Corwin still hasn't named his need. Giselle's crew still hasn't framed a wall. And I'm standing here asking questions when the only answer that matters is whether the morning finds me with enough to pay what's owed.

output:
*Ezra Lund sits at the edge of his household's threshold, counting the flour in his hands like a man counting debts. The morning is new but the weight is old. Two people, 180 upkeep, 60 tax. 3663 sim in hand. The math is simple enough even before the coffee. He could cover today, and tomorrow, and the day after—but only counting flour won't fill bellies and only sitting still won't earn.*

Household's solvent, sure. Solvent means the bills get paid. It doesn't mean we thrive.

*He stands, brushes the mill-dust from his trousers—habit, though he wasn't milling last night—and considers the inventory. Timber and planks want selling. The election's coming. Giselle's trench work wants materials. And somewhere in this town, someone needs what he's holding.*

*His jaw sets. No promises made yet today, so none to break. That's the rule.*

First, he thinks, I find out what the day actually wants from me. Then I decide if I'm willing to give it.

*The empty house holds no answers. The street might.* *He sets his mind to the work, same as he'd set a dovetail. Clear, measured, meant to hold.*  *Arrived at the yard. The smell of sawn wood and honest labor.*  *Idris Solano stands alone at Giselle's yard. The trench work, if it's still going, needs what I'm holding. Question is whether Idris is buying or just standing guard over other people's orders.*  *He waits, weight on his back foot, the way he always does when the deal hasn't shown its shape yet.*
